entries.onMind: the blank west side of the map
entries.text: Dreamed I was pacing a line across the map sheet itself, the pencil walking ahead of me. Every hundred paces the paper unrolled a little more, and I woke before I could read what was on it.
entries.title: The pacing count

entries.text: The inside of the dome is beaded all over from the damp night, but through it the float sits square on its north notch and the water still humps over the rim. A whole night and it didn't dry down.
entries.title: Beads inside the glass

entries.text: Ate three handfuls of halves at the shallows and couldn't find the bitter anywhere. The fog is so thick on the water I can't see the far bank from the stones.
entries.title: No bitter at all

entries.onMind: a first trunk on the line west, and something at camp to look back at
queries: how to walk a straight line through woods without a compass
entries.query: how to walk a straight line through woods without a compass
entries.reason: The compass floats in a lid of water on the bench and can't come with him on the walk west.
entries.source: Sensible Survival: Maintaining a Straight Course in the Wilderness
entries.text: People walk in circles because one leg pulls a little harder. The fix is to pick a mark straight ahead, walk to it, look back at where you started, and pick the next one in line, tree to tree in a forest. Slow, but it holds a line.
entries.title: Tree to tree

entries.text: Laid my eye along the needle under the dome and followed its west end out past the scrap pile. The line runs into gray at the water. Not one trunk to pick. The walk waits on the fog.
entries.title: Nothing to sight on

entries.text: Tore a strip off the lid's old shade canvas and tied it to the top of the lantern post. From across the creek I'll need to see where I started, and the post is the tallest straight thing in camp.
entries.title: A flag for looking back

queries: compass you can carry without water hang magnetized needle on thread
entries.query: compass you can carry without water hang magnetized needle on thread
entries.reason: The floating needle can't leave the bench, and the walk west needs a compass that can.
entries.text: An old army trick: stroke a needle on a magnet and hang it from a piece of thread or a long hair, any string that isn't metal, and it swings round to north. The page never says how to balance it or keep it still, so that part is mine to find out.
entries.title: Hang it from a hair

entries.text: Stroked a spare sliver forty times down the lodestone, one way only, and tied a strand of stalk cord around its middle. Four tries to find the spot where it hangs level.
entries.title: Spare sliver

entries.onMind: something to hang it from that has no twist
entries.text: Held it up by the cord. It never settles: turns one way, stops, turns back, round and round. The cord is twisted and it's unwinding itself through the needle, while the floater on the bench sits steady the whole time.
entries.title: It won't hold still

entries.text: The page said thread or a long hair. I've got a head full of hair.
entries.title: A hair, then

entries.onMind: keeping air off a hung needle
entries.text: Pulled a hair from the top of my head and tied it round the sliver with one knot. It turns slower than on the cord, stops, swings back past, and after a slow count of sixty it rests along the same line as the floater. Then I breathed on it and it went off again.
entries.title: One hair

queries: hanging magnetized needle on a hair keeps swinging how to stop it
suspended needle compass inside a jar out of the wind
entries.query: hanging magnetized needle on a hair keeps swinging how to stop it
entries.reason: His hair-hung needle found north but swung off again at a breath, and the walk west needs a needle he can carry.
entries.source: Kharisma Bangsa Physics Project: Jar Compass
entries.text: First search turned up nothing I could use. The second found a school project: push the needle through a scrap of card, tie a thread to the card and the other end to the middle of a pencil, and lay the pencil across the mouth of a jar so the needle hangs inside. The page never says why the jar. Out of the wind is my guess.
entries.title: A needle in a jar

entries.onMind: something that holds a hair inside glass
entries.text: I have a pencil the right length to lay across a jar. The honey jar cracked crooked, and the dome is a jar the wrong way up, with no mouth on top to hang anything from.
entries.title: Wrong way up

entries.onMind: the line west running past someone's fire
entries.text: Ate a handful of halves at the shallows. The fog is off the water and I can see the far bank clear for the first time today: between the big trunks, a little upstream of the stones, a ring of gray stones on a bare swept patch with a long log beside it, and no smoke. That's where the smoke comes from, and it sits almost due west of my bench.
entries.title: Due west of camp

entries.onMind: walking to mark one and looking back at the flag
entries.text: Laid my eye along the needle under the dome. Its west end points over the stones at a huge trunk on the far bank with a pale scar of bark about shoulder height, a few strides north of that stone ring. That's mark one.
entries.title: First trunk

entries.onMind: the blank west side of the map
entries.text: Drew the flag post, the creek, the stepping stones, the scarred trunk with a 1 beside it, and a small circle of stones just south of it marked 'someone's fire, not mine'. West of that the sheet is still blank.
entries.title: On the sheet

entries.text: Counted out loud across the stones and up the far bank: forty-one paces from the flag post to the scarred trunk. Looked back and the flag is a gray speck on the post. Straight opposite it, west, is a flat stump past the stone ring, so that's mark two.
entries.title: Forty-one

entries.text: Walked by the stone ring on the way. Cold gray ash, leaves swept back off a bare circle, and an empty tray of folded bark sitting at the edge of the ash. Somebody here cooks. I didn't touch any of it.
entries.title: Not my fire

entries.text: Mark two is a stump cut flat at about my waist, with a rack of straight sticks stood up beside it and pale shavings in the leaves. Drew it on the sheet and wrote 'someone's bench'. Whoever has the fire works here too.
entries.title: Someone's bench

entries.text: Facing west from the bench, the breeze in my face smells of salt, like the jerky did. The light between the trunks ahead is white and flat, and under the leaves there's a low roar that isn't in the treetops.
entries.title: Salt on the wind

entries.text: About eighty paces past the bench the trees quit and so does the ground. A rock lip, and a long way below it, water out to the edge of the sky, gray-blue and moving, with rock towers standing in it and white birds on them. No far side.
entries.title: The ground stops

entries.text: Everyone at home said the land ends at a cliff into an ocean. It does. I walked all this way to prove them wrong and I'm standing on the exact thing they said.
entries.title: They weren't lying

entries.text: Drew a hard line down the whole west side of the sheet and hatched the drop. Past it I wrote 'water, no far side seen'. My map now goes farther west than any of my people's, and it stops in the same place.
entries.title: The west edge of the sheet

entries.text: They said there's no west. There is one. It's water, and it goes on. Nobody at home ever said what's on the other side, because nobody ever stood here and looked. The wings were always for this.
entries.title: Not 'nothing'

entries.reason: Anything that stays up without working at it is the thing the wings need to learn.
entries.text: Lay on my stomach and watched the white birds below the lip. Three of them hang in the wind just off the rock, wings out, and don't beat once for a slow count of thirty. Then one tips and slides off sideways, still not flapping.
entries.title: Birds that don't flap

queries: birds hang in the air without flapping at a cliff edge wind
entries.query: birds hang in the air without flapping at a cliff edge wind
entries.reason: He watched birds hang in the wind below the lip without a wingbeat.
entries.source: Lake Champlain Committee: Nature Note – Soaring
entries.text: Gulls and hawks stay up without flapping on rising air, and one kind comes off 'geographic obstructions like cliffs or mountains'. The same rising air keeps gliders up. The page never says how, but the wind in my face is coming straight off the water into this rock wall, and it has to go somewhere.
entries.title: Lift off a cliff

queries: how tall is a cliff drop a rock and count the seconds
entries.query: how tall is a cliff drop a rock and count the seconds
entries.reason: He wanted to know how far down the water is before he puts a number on the map.
entries.source: Gizmodo: The Easy Way to Know the Height of the Cliff You're Jumping Off
entries.text: To get a cliff's height, drop a rock and time it to the water, square the seconds and multiply by sixteen for feet. Rough, but it's math I can do in my head. No stopwatch, so I'll have to count.
entries.title: Sixteen times the square

entries.onMind: The air goes up the wall. That's what the birds are sitting on.
entries.text: Held a dry leaf out past the lip and let go. It dropped a hand, stopped, and came back up past my face and over my shoulder into the trees. Did it again with two more. Every one went up.
entries.title: The leaf came back

entries.onMind: A hundred feet of rising air under the lip, and my frame has never left the stand.
entries.text: Let three pebbles go from the lip and counted one-thousand to each splash. Two and a half every time, near enough. Two and a half squared is six and a quarter, times sixteen: a hundred feet, give or take my counting. Wrote it on the sheet by the edge line.
entries.title: About a hundred feet

entries.onMind: which way the wind has to blow
entries.text: The wind went round. It comes from the north now, along the rock instead of into it. Let a leaf go and it dropped, slid south down the face and was gone; two more did the same. The white birds are flapping now, and two of them have left.
entries.title: The leaf went down

entries.onMind: a wind rule on the sheet
queries: does wind have to blow straight at a cliff for birds to glide on it
entries.query: does wind have to blow straight at a cliff for birds to glide on it
entries.reason: An hour ago the leaves came back up over the lip; with the wind gone round to the north they fall.
entries.text: Lift off a cliff only happens when the wind blows against the face and gets shoved up it, strongest straight out from the rock. Wind running along it gives nothing. And near a sheer drop the air at the bottom is rough and sinking. So the glide only works on a wind off the water.
entries.title: Only wind at the face

entries.text: Drew the rock towers below the edge, five that I can count, and beside the edge line wrote 'lift only with wind off the water, not along'. One hour of a west wind and I nearly thought it was always there.
entries.title: Five towers

entries.onMind: walking the line back to the shallows to eat
entries.text: Nothing in me since the halves at the shallows, and the net bag is on the other side of the whole forest. The birds that are left sit on the towers with their wings folded, waiting on the wind same as me.
entries.title: Empty since the shallows

queries: how far can you see out to sea from 100 feet up
entries.query: how far can you see out to sea from 100 feet up
entries.reason: He wants to know how much 'no far side' actually rules out.
entries.source: Pajack: From How Far Can You See A Lighthouse?
entries.text: From a hundred feet up, the edge of the water is about thirteen miles off: square root of seven times the height, over four. So 'no far side seen' only means nothing inside thirteen miles. Whatever is out there could sit just past where the water bends away.
entries.title: Thirteen miles

entries.text: My people said there's nothing out there. None of them ever stood up here. The most anybody can say from this rock is: nothing for thirteen miles.
entries.title: Nothing for thirteen miles

entries.text: Paced it back from the lip to the flat stump, counting out loud: eighty-three. Wrote it on the sheet between the edge line and 'someone's bench', and out in the blank past the edge, 'about 13 miles to where the water ends, from the top'.
entries.title: Eighty-three back

entries.text: Forty-one paces from the scarred trunk back to the flag, same as this morning, so the line holds both ways. Lifted the stone off the net bag at the shallows and ate four handfuls of halves before I sat down.
entries.title: Forty-one again

entries.text: Two more handfuls and the shaking in my hands is gone. The net bag is down to maybe a third. Set the stone back on it; I'll need more acorns off the east oak before long.
entries.title: Two more handfuls

entries.text: Picked up acorns under the east oak, thirty-one, and threw back four with holes in them. Fresh ones get their own soak; the bag in the shallows is nearly sweet and I'm not undoing that.
entries.title: Under the east oak

entries.text: Knocked them open on the plank bench with the flat of the wrench, twenty-seven good ones, and dropped the halves into the dented tin with creek water over them. Two days at least before they're worth eating.
entries.title: Halves in the tin

queries: how to balance a compass needle on a pin so it can turn dry
entries.query: how to balance a compass needle on a pin so it can turn dry
entries.reason: The floater can't leave the bench, and he wants a needle that turns without water so he can carry it west.
entries.source: Chest of Books: A Substitute For A Compass (The Boy Mechanic)
entries.text: An old shop book pushes the needle through a cork, sticks a pin through it crosswise, and angles two sharpened matches down from the sides so the weight hangs low; then the whole thing sits on a thimble without tipping. Level it by sliding the needle or adding wax. Weight below the point is what keeps it upright.
entries.title: A needle on a point

entries.text: No cork and no thimble. But a plug of stalk pith, the spare sliver, two splinters hanging down off the sides and a hard point under the middle: every part of that is on this bench or in the scrap.
entries.title: Pith, not cork

entries.text: Whittling a point on a hardwood splinter out of the scrap pile for it to sit on. Too soft and the pith will sink onto it and stick; too sharp and it'll punch straight through.
entries.title: A point to sit on

entries.text: Pushed the spare sliver crosswise through a plug of stalk pith the size of my thumb tip. Push fast and the pith crumbles; went slow, a hair at a time.
entries.title: Sliver through pith

entries.text: Tied two splinters to hang off the sides so the weight sits low, like the shop book said, and set the plug on the new point. The north end ducked and the whole thing slid off onto the bench. Four tries, same end every time.
entries.title: North end ducks

queries: homemade dry compass needle on a pin keeps tipping over to one side how to fix
entries.query: homemade dry compass needle on a pin keeps tipping over to one side how to fix
entries.reason: The balanced needle tipped north-end-down four times out of four.
entries.source: Outdoors Codidact: How do simple compass needles remain level instead of see-sawing with magnetic dip?
entries.text: A magnetized needle doesn't just swing toward north, it gets pulled down at the north end too, more the farther north you are. Compass makers balance the needle against that for the part of the world it's sold in; a needle balanced for one place drags in another. So it isn't my knots.
entries.title: North pulls down too

entries.text: Before the stone touched it, the sliver sat level. It was the magnet that tipped it. Every compass is a little bit about where you are standing.
entries.title: Balanced for here

entries.text: Wound three turns of thin cord round the south end as a counterweight. Now it sits almost level on the point and turns, slow, and stops short: twice out of three near the notch. Sticky, but it stays up.
entries.title: Upright, sticky

entries.text: Lifted the stone off the net bag and ate three handfuls of halves squatting on the bank. Down to about a quarter now; the tin batch had better hurry.
entries.title: Down to a quarter

queries: compass needle sticks on the pin point how to make it turn freely
compass needle jewel cap pivot bearing why needle has a cup on the point
entries.query: compass needle sticks on the pin point how to make it turn freely
entries.reason: The dry needle turns but stops short, as if the point catches.
entries.text: First page only said the point has to be nearly frictionless, which I knew. The second said a real needle pivots on a jewel bearing: something hard and smooth under it, not soft pith. My pith is sinking onto the point and grabbing it.
entries.title: A seat under the point

entries.text: No jewels in the scrap pile. Dug out a corner of thin tin off an old can, about a thumbnail across, and flattened it under my boot.
entries.title: No jewels here

entries.text: Looked up from the vise: thin smoke leaning north over the trees past the water, right where the stone ring is. The fire keeper's home. Haven't seen who.
entries.title: Smoke past the water

entries.text: Set the scrap on the end of a stick and tapped it with the wrench until it took a small round dent, then pressed the dent up into the bottom of the pith plug, cup side down.
entries.title: A dent for a seat

entries.text: Set it on the point with the tin seat under it. It swings, overshoots, swings back and settles on the notch, three out of three. Still shivers if I breathe on it, but it isn't sticking. Sun's getting low.
entries.title: Three out of three

entries.onMind: whether the dry needle works off the bench
entries.reason: He wants to see whether the dry needle works anywhere but his bench, and the sun is getting low.
entries.text: Wrapped the plug, its tin seat and the hardwood point in a scrap of canvas and put a slice of bread in my shirt. Smoke is still going up off the stone ring, right on my line west, so I'll go round by the stump instead of walking through somebody's supper.
entries.title: Wide of the fire

entries.text: Went up the far bank well north of the stone ring: orange light low between the trunks to my left and wood smoke, nobody in sight. Set the wrench down on the stump top to free my hands and it knocked loud on the wood. Stood still a while. Nothing came.
entries.title: A knock on the stump

entries.onMind: why the sun sits left of west
entries.text: Unwrapped the plug and set it on its point on the stump. Four swings and it settled, and it held when I stepped back. The low sun sits a good hand left of where the needle puts west. Either the needle's off or the sun is.
entries.title: Off the bench

entries.text: Breeze from the south, running along the face. The white birds are flapping below the lip, none of them hanging. Same as this afternoon: wind along the rock gives nothing.
entries.title: Wind along the rock

queries: does the sun set due west in november
entries.query: does the sun set due west in november
entries.reason: On the stump the sun sat well left of the needle's west and he needed to know which one to trust.
entries.source: Almanac.com: Where Does the Sun Set? (Hint: It's Not Always Due West)
entries.text: The sun only sets due west twice a year, at the equinoxes. In fall it drifts south every evening and sets southwest of west, farthest at midwinter. So the needle was right on the stump and the sun is the one that wanders.
entries.title: Left of west

entries.text: Ate the slice of bread at the edge and watched the sun go down into the water a hand left of west, just like the page said. The loaf is down to the heel.
entries.title: Into the water

entries.text: Back home they say the sun drowns out there every night. It doesn't even drown in the same place twice. Whatever is past thirteen miles, the sun knows the way.
entries.title: It goes somewhere

entries.onMind: the fire keeper heard me, maybe
entries.text: Left the edge with the last light and no lantern, which was dumb. Under the trees it went dark fast; the glow of the stone-ring fire kept my line, and I gave it a wide berth to the north. Leaves loud underfoot the whole way, and the wrench clinked on my belt.
entries.title: Home by their fire

entries.onMind: the second batch in the tin
entries.text: Found the net bag's stone in the shallows by feel and scooped two handfuls of halves. Cold water, cold fingers. The bag is down to a fifth.
entries.title: Supper by feel

entries.text: Lit the lantern at the end of the bench and left the other two dark. The oil can sloshes a little under half; next time I go to the edge I take a lantern with me.
entries.title: One lantern

entries.text: Ate on the crate. The needle said west and the sun went down a hand left of it, and the needle was right. Tomorrow that goes on the map: where the sun drowns, by date.
entries.title: Left of west

entries.onMind: wind off the water for a glide
entries.text: Wind came round out of the north and the wing frame started knocking on its stand. Put a frap on the rear side-spar joint, four turns cinched between spar and frame. It quit ticking.
entries.title: Rear joint frapped

entries.text: Drew a short line off the edge of the sheet from where I sat, a hand left of west, and wrote the date beside it. One line. If I put one down every clear night I'll see how far it walks.
entries.title: First sunset line

entries.text: Set the glass dome over the dry needle on its point. The north wind is shoving the tarp around and rattling the lantern post; under the glass the needle didn't shiver once.
entries.title: Under the glass

entries.onMind: a tin floor for the dome
entries.text: Glass on top, needle in the middle, and it still stands on my bench. It needs a flat round floor the dome can sit on so the whole thing goes in my pouch. Something tin, shallow.
entries.title: Needs a floor

entries.text: Dug the hand-wide piece of tin back out of the scrap pile by lantern, folded corner, spoon dent and all. A loose sheet slid down the pile with a clatter that went on longer than I liked.
entries.title: Back to the bent tin

entries.text: No orange past the water tonight, not even a red glow. Whoever keeps that fire put it to bed early, or the north wind did it for them.
entries.title: Dark past the water

entries.text: Laid the tin across the vise jaws at the far end of the bench, away from the needle, and beat it with the wrench. The fold opened and the spoon dent came out to a shallow wave. Where the fold was, a ridge a fingernail high won't go down.
entries.title: Hammered flat, mostly

entries.text: Set the glass dome down on the hammered tin. It rocks on the ridge, with a gap under one side I could slide a stalk into. And even flat, the hardwood point needs something to stand it up in the middle.
entries.title: Rocks on the ridge

entries.text: Ate the last of the halves I scooped this evening, on the crate. Tomorrow the net bag needs filling, or the tin batch has to be ready.
entries.title: Last of the scoop

entries.reason: The dome rocked on the fold's ridge, and a compass that rocks in the pouch is no compass.
entries.text: Turned the tin over and beat the ridge down from underneath with the wrench, short taps all along it. It's down to a hair now; the dome only rocks if I press on one edge.
entries.title: Ridge from underneath

entries.text: The orange is back past the water, small and low between the trunks, after an hour of dark. Somebody came back out to it once the wind quit.
entries.title: Orange again

entries.text: Whittled a foot out of a hardwood offcut, flat on the bottom, and bored a hole in the top with the knife point so the hardwood point stands up in it.
entries.title: A foot for the point

entries.text: Ate the heel of the loaf on the crate, slow. That's the last of the bread.
entries.title: Heel of the loaf

entries.onMind: cutting the foot down a thumb
entries.text: Stood the point in the foot, set the needle on it, and put the dome over the lot on the tin. The north end ducks and scrapes the glass wall every swing; the foot puts it a thumb too high. Tomorrow it gets cut down.
entries.title: Too tall by a thumb

entries.text: The orange past the water sank to a red spot and went out, not long after it came back. Same as the other nights: whoever keeps it buries it before they sleep.
entries.title: Out again

entries.text: Whittled the foot down by a thumb, a few shavings at a time, holding it up against the dome after every pass. Stopped when the point's tip sat just under the middle of the glass.
entries.title: A thumb off the foot

entries.text: Needle back on the point, dome over it. The north end clears the wall by a fingernail now, swings, and settles on the same line as the floating one did. It hangs up a hair before it stops; a tap on the tin and it finishes the swing.
entries.title: Clears the glass

entries.text: Twisted an arm's length of stalk cord on the crate for a sling, so the tin, the foot and the dome can hang off my belt instead of living on the bench. If it rides on me, it walks west with me.
entries.title: Cord for a sling

entries.text: Wound the cord twice round the tin under its rim and tied it off with a loop big enough for my belt. The dome sits inside the wraps so it can't walk off the floor.
entries.title: A sling on the tin

entries.onMind: keeping the needle on its point when the tin swings
entries.reason: A compass that only works sitting still on a bench can't walk west with him.
entries.text: Hung it on my belt and stood up off the crate. The tin swung, the needle hopped off the point and rattled round under the glass like a bug in a jar. On the bench it's a compass; on me it's a rattle.
entries.title: Off the point

entries.text: Found the stone on the net bag by feel and scooped two handfuls of halves. The bag is down to a tenth. Past the water, no orange at all; whoever keeps that fire put it to bed hours ago.
entries.title: Net bag by feel

entries.text: Ate the halves on the bank in the cold. The low owl gave its five hoots over the water and nothing answered. Maybe the needle needs a little cap on top so it can't jump, the way a hat stays on a head.
entries.title: Low one, no answer

entries.reason: Last night the needle hopped off its point as soon as the tin swung.
entries.text: Lifted the pith plug off the point and set its tin seat on a stick end at the bench. Tapped the dent deeper with the wrench until it was a cup instead of a saucer; now it sits down over the point like a cap.
entries.title: A deeper seat

entries.onMind: how real pocket compasses keep their needles on
entries.text: Hung the tin back on my belt and swung it five times sitting on the crate. On the easy swings the needle rode it out and came back to its line; on the two hard ones it jumped and rattled. Better than a rattle every time. Still not a compass you can walk with.
entries.title: Two hops in five

entries.text: Deeper cup, lighter needle, or I just stop and hold the tin still when I want a reading. Turned the bench lantern down and out to save oil. When the sun's up I'll ask the tablet how the pocket kind keep their needles on.
entries.title: Ask in the morning
